plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two orbital drawings of a carbon-carbon double bond separated by a labeled arrow, before and after a twist. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" are stacked diagonally, each drawn with a pink lobe above and a blue lobe below, the lobes tapering to points at the carbon and each pink lobe carrying a small black dot. The two sets are parallel, and thin straight lines run along the outer edges of the upper pink pair and the lower blue pair to show that the lobes line up so their broad faces overlap sideways; short black bars and dashed lines at each carbon mark the remaining bonds and the plane they occupy. A horizontal arrow across the middle is labeled "rotate 90°". On the right the lower carbon is unchanged, but the upper one has been turned so its pink lobe points toward the viewer at the left and its blue lobe away at the right, leaving the two pairs crossing at right angles instead of running parallel. Bold labels beneath read "π bond (p orbitals are parallel)" and "Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)". Setting the aligned lobes against the crossed ones makes sideways overlap the thing to watch, explaining why twisting such a bond costs the full strength of the pi bond and so does not happen freely.

elements: Left p-orbital (pink top lobe with black dot, blue bottom lobe, fixed vertically)
Right p-orbital (pink top lobe with black dot, blue bottom lobe, rotates around C-C axis)
Left carbon sigma bonds (black wedge and dashed line)
Right carbon sigma bonds (black wedge and dashed line, rotates with right carbon)
C-C rotation axis (faint dashed line connecting the two carbons)
Parallel overlap indicator lines (connecting the lobe tips)
Overlap strength indicator (dynamic text showing π-bond strength percentage)

Allows spatial inspection of the orbital alignment from different viewing angles.

demo_steps.title: Parallel p orbitals
demo_steps.narration: At 0°, the p orbitals are perfectly parallel. Their broad side-by-side overlap forms a strong, intact π bond.

demo_steps.title: Broken π bond
demo_steps.narration: Rotating the carbon to 90° makes the p orbitals perpendicular, completely breaking the overlap. This high energy cost prevents free rotation around double bonds.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Left C placed at (-1.5, 0, 0), Right C at (1.5, 0, 0). The camera's perspective azimuth and elevation will naturally make the Right C appear higher and further back, exactly mimicking the 2D source drawing. p-orbitals are teardrop shapes extending ±1.5 units along their local Y-axis (max radius ~0.7). Colors: Pink #ea5b76, Blue #4a90e2. Black dots on the pink lobes sit on the outer surface (local Y~0.8, Z~0.7). Substituent bonds on Left C extend ~1 unit toward roughly (-1, 0, 1) and (-1, 0, -1); on Right C toward (1, 0, 1) and (1, 0, -1). Right C, its p-orbital, and its substituents all rotate together around the X-axis by `rotationAngle`. Overlap indicator lines run from (-1.5, 1.5, 0) to (1.5, 1.5, 0) and (-1.5, -1.5, 0) to (1.5, -1.5, 0). Overlap strength percentage is 100 * cos(rotationAngle).
interactionPlan.notes: Tie the rotation of the entire right-hand carbon assembly (orbital, label, and sigma bonds) to the slider value as a rotation around the global X-axis. Scale the opacity of the parallel overlap indicator lines by cos(rotationAngle) so they fade out as the bond breaks. Update the dynamic text indicator reactively.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for rotating the upper carbon from 0 to 90 degrees; the p orbitals move from parallel overlap to perpendicular separation while an overlap or pi-bond-strength indicator falls, making pi-bond breaking the cost of rotation.

authoredContext:
Although essentially free rotation around single bonds is possible (another section), the same is not true of double bonds. For rotation to occur around a double bond, the π bond must break and re-form (the figure). Thus, the barrier to double-bond rotation must be at least as great as the strength of the π bond itself, an estimated 350 kJ/mol (84 kcal/mol). Recall that the barrier to bond rotation in ethane is only 12 kJ/mol.

The π bond must break for rotation to take place around a carbon–carbon double bond.

An orbital diagram with two parallel p orbitals before rotation. After rotation the p orbitals are perpendicular, which breaks the double bond.

The lack of rotation around carbon–carbon double bonds is of more than just theoretical interest; it also has chemical consequences. Imagine the situation for a disubstituted alkene such as 2-butene. (Disubstituted means that two substituents other than hydrogen are bonded to the double-bond carbons.) The two methyl groups in 2-butene can either be on the same side of the double bond or on opposite sides, a situation similar to that in disubstituted cycloalkanes (another section).

discrepancies: The black dots representing electrons are placed awkwardly on the outer surface edge rather than centered on the front of the pink lobes.
The solid black lines indicating pi-bond overlap remain fixed in space when the right orbital is rotated, rather than tracking its physical tips.
The colors of the orbitals are darker and less vibrant compared to the luminous pink and blue of the source figure.
The stereochemical wedge bonds are rendered as elongated 3D cones rather than standard 2D wedge shapes.
evaluation.notes: The interactive adaptation is conceptually excellent and the UI controls perfectly capture the two states of the original static figure, though some minor geometric details (overlap lines failing to track rotation, dot placement, lighting) need refinement.
action_items: In updateRotation(), dynamically update the vertices of topOverlap and botOverlap so they continuously connect to the tips of the right orbital as it rotates.
Adjust the local position of the black dots (e.g., decrease the Z coordinate) so they sit centrally on the pink lobes without appearing to float off the edge.
Increase ambient light intensity and tweak material colors to better match the bright, vibrant pink and blue of the source image.

feedback.rationale: The scores are excellent across the board with no failure modes, indicating the interactive figure is highly successful and minor visual polish is not worth further iteration.
